slides.heading: Marketing Mix: Place and Promotion
slides.body_md: Part 1: **channels of distribution**, their **levels**, how to **choose** one, and **physical distribution**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: channels of distribution, zero-, one- and two-level channels, factors in choosing a channel, and the elements of physical distribution
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A good product at the right price is of no use if buyers cannot find it. Place, the third P, is about getting goods to buyers. In this part we look at channels of distribution, how to choose one, and the physical tasks of moving goods.

slides.heading: What is a channel of distribution?
slides.body_md: A **channel of distribution** is the route through which goods pass from the **producer to the final buyer**, with the **middlemen** involved.

rows: Buys in bulk, stores, sells in smaller lots to retailers
Sells to final consumers in small quantities
Holds stock or arranges sales in an area

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of middlemen and what each does

slides.narration: Goods often pass through middlemen on their way to buyers. Wholesalers buy in bulk, store goods and sell smaller lots to retailers. Retailers sell to final consumers. Middlemen break bulk, give credit and spread goods widely, so they perform useful functions, not just add cost.

visual.caption: The level of a channel is the number of middlemen in it.

slides.narration: The level of a channel is the number of middlemen in it. A zero-level channel has none: the maker sells directly. A one-level channel has a retailer. A two-level channel has a wholesaler and a retailer, and suits goods bought often by many buyers.

bullets: Step 1: trace the **route** of the goods.
Step 2: **count** the middlemen.
Step 3: name the level.

rows: Jaggery maker selling at its farm-gate shop
Saree weaver selling through city boutiques

visual.alt: Worked table: three imagined firms, the route their goods take, and the level of channel
visual.caption: Count the middlemen between the maker and the consumer.

slides.narration: A jaggery maker selling at its own farm-gate shop has no middleman, so it is zero-level. A saree weaver selling through city boutiques has one, the retailer, so it is one-level. A bakery whose macaroons go to stockists and then sweet shops has two, so it is two-level.

slides.heading: Choosing a channel

headers: Points towards a short channel when…
Points towards a long channel when…
rows: Perishable, costly, technical or made to order

visual.alt: Table of four groups of factors in choosing a channel, showing when each points towards a short channel and when towards a long one

slides.narration: Four groups of factors guide the choice. Product: perishable, costly or technical goods need short channels. Market: a few large buyers close together can be served directly. Company: a firm with strong finances can sell directly, while a small firm relies on middlemen. Competition: firms often use the channels their rivals use.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which factor?
bullets: Step 1: decide which **group** the fact belongs to.
Step 2: say whether it pushes towards a **short or long** channel.
Step 3: suggest the channel.

rows: Coconut water spoils in two days
Twelve buyer mills in one town
New firm, little capital, no sales staff
Rivals all sell in hotel gift shops

visual.alt: Worked table: four imagined situations, the factor each shows, and the channel suggested
visual.caption: Name the factor first, then say which way it pushes the channel.

slides.narration: Coconut water that spoils in two days is a product factor, calling for a short channel. Twelve buyer mills in one town is a market factor, allowing direct selling. A new firm with little capital is a company factor, so it uses middlemen. Rivals in hotel gift shops is a competitive factor.

slides.body_md: A jaggery maker sells only at its own farm-gate shop and from its own van. Which channel is this?
slides.narration: Is there anyone between the maker and the buyer?

slides.heading: Physical distribution
slides.body_md: **Physical distribution** covers the activities that move goods physically from the producer to buyers at the **right place and time**.

visual.alt: Four elements of physical distribution: order processing, warehousing, inventory control and transportation
visual.caption: Physical distribution gets goods to buyers at the right place and time.

slides.narration: Choosing a channel decides who handles the goods. Physical distribution is about actually moving them. Orders must be processed, goods stored in warehouses near markets, the right stock kept, and goods transported to buyers. We need only the meaning of each element.

slides.heading: Elements of physical distribution

rows: Invoice raised and cartons packed the same day
Keeping the right level of stock
Minimum and maximum stock for each size

visual.alt: Table of the four elements of physical distribution with their meanings and an imagined example of each

slides.narration: Order processing means receiving, checking and preparing orders. Transportation means moving goods to buyers. Warehousing means storing them near markets. Inventory control means keeping the right level of stock, neither so little that sales are lost nor so much that money is locked up.

slides.heading: Quick check: storing near markets
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: keeping goods in godowns near markets until needed is called ___.
slides.narration: One word, one of the four elements.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Route of goods from maker to buyer, with middlemen
Product, market, company and competitive factors
Order processing, transportation, warehousing, inventory control

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: channels, levels, factors in choosing a channel and physical distribution

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. A channel of distribution is the route of goods from maker to buyer. Zero-level has no middleman, one-level has a retailer, and two-level has a wholesaler and a retailer. Product, market, company and competitive factors guide the choice. Physical distribution covers order processing, transportation, warehousing and inventory control.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: **Draw** each channel as a flow with arrows.
The level equals the **number of middlemen**.
Name the **factor group** before explaining it.
For physical distribution, the **meaning** of each element is enough.

nodes.label: Name the channel, element or tool

slides.narration: Some tips. Draw channels as simple flows with arrows. Remember that the level is the number of middlemen. When explaining factors, say whether each is a product, market, company or competitive factor. For physical distribution, a clear meaning of each element is enough.

decks.title: Place and Promotion — Part 2: The Promotion Mix
goals: Explain the promotion mix and its role in informing and persuading customers
Compare advertising with personal selling, and sales promotion with publicity
Recommend a suitable promotion element for a given product and market

slides.heading: The Promotion Mix
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **promotion mix**, its **roles**, the four **tools**, how they **differ**, and how to **choose** among them.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the promotion mix, advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, publicity, and choosing the right tool
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Promotion is the fourth P. It is how a firm tells buyers about its product and persuades them to buy. In this part we meet the four tools of promotion, see how they differ, and learn how to choose the right one.

slides.heading: Promotion mix and its roles
slides.body_md: The **promotion mix** is the combination of **advertising, sales promotion, personal selling and publicity** a firm uses.

visual.alt: Three roles of promotion: inform, persuade and remind
visual.caption: New products need informing; rival products need persuading; familiar products need reminding.

slides.narration: Promotion has three roles. For a new product, it informs buyers that it exists and what it does. Where rivals compete, it persuades buyers to choose this product. For a familiar product, it reminds buyers so that it stays in their minds.

slides.heading: Quick check: four tools together
slides.body_md: A firm uses advertisements, a festival discount, salespeople at exhibitions and a news story. Together these are its…
slides.narration: Which mix combines all four tools?

slides.heading: The four tools

rows: Paid, impersonal message by an identified sponsor
A television film or magazine page
Unpaid, non-personal coverage in the media
A newspaper feature on the firm

visual.alt: Table of the four promotion tools with the meaning of each and a typical example

slides.narration: Advertising is a paid, impersonal message from an identified sponsor. Sales promotion offers short-term incentives such as coupons and free samples. Personal selling is a face-to-face, two-way presentation to buyers. Publicity is unpaid coverage in the media, which the firm does not control.

slides.heading: Advertising versus personal selling
columns:
**Advertising**

Impersonal, one-way, reaches many, low cost per person.

**Personal selling**

Face to face, two-way, reaches few, high cost per person, flexible.

visual.alt: Table distinguishing advertising from personal selling on contact, communication, reach, cost per person and flexibility

slides.narration: Advertising sends one message to very many people at a low cost per person, but cannot answer questions. Personal selling talks to a few people at a time, at a high cost per person, but it is two-way and can be adapted to each buyer.

slides.heading: Sales promotion versus publicity
columns:
**Sales promotion**

Paid and controlled by the firm; short-term push to sales.

**Publicity**

Unpaid; controlled by the media; builds credibility over time.

slides.narration: Sales promotion is paid for and controlled by the firm, and it aims at quick sales through offers. Publicity costs nothing, but the media decide what to say. Because it comes from an independent source, buyers often find it more believable.

notes.title: Marketing Mix: Place and Promotion — notes

sections.heading: 1. Channels of distribution
sections.body_md:
A **channel of distribution** is the route, with its **middlemen**, through which goods pass from the producer to the final buyer. Middlemen (wholesalers, retailers, agents) break bulk, store, give credit, assemble assortments and reach scattered buyers.

**Levels:**
- **Zero-level (direct):** Manufacturer → Consumer (own shops, door-to-door, own website).
- **One-level:** Manufacturer → Retailer → Consumer.
- **Two-level:** Manufacturer → Wholesaler → Retailer → Consumer.

**Factors in choosing a channel:**
- **Product** — perishability, unit value, technical nature, standard or made to order.
- **Market** — number and size of buyers, their location, size of orders, consumer or industrial buyers.
- **Company** — financial strength, desire for control, own sales staff.
- **Competition** — channels used by rivals.

sections.heading: 2. Physical distribution (meaning only)
sections.body_md:
**Physical distribution** covers the activities involved in moving goods physically from the producer to buyers at the right place and time.

**Elements:**
- **Order processing** — receiving, checking and preparing orders for dispatch.
- **Transportation** — moving goods to where buyers are.
- **Warehousing** — storing goods, often near markets, until needed.
- **Inventory control** — maintaining the right level of stock: enough to meet orders without locking up too much money.

sections.heading: 4. The four promotion tools and their differences
sections.body_md:
**Advertising** — a paid, impersonal form of communication about a product by an **identified sponsor**. Features: paid, impersonal, one-way, wide reach, low cost per person. Objectives: inform, persuade, remind, build image, support salespeople.

**Sales promotion** — **short-term incentives** to encourage immediate buying: discounts, coupons, free samples, contests, quantity offers, gifts. It supplements advertising and personal selling.

**Personal selling** — **face-to-face, two-way** presentation to prospective buyers to make a sale. Features: personal contact, flexibility, relationship building, immediate feedback; high cost per buyer.

**Publicity** — **unpaid, non-personal** coverage of a firm or product in the media; not controlled by the firm but highly credible.

**Choosing a tool:** few buyers or technical, costly products → personal selling; a large, scattered market → advertising; quick sales or clearing stock → sales promotion; a newsworthy story → publicity.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain zero-level, one-level and two-level channels of distribution, with an imagined example of each. [3]

questions.solution_md: Three channels with examples; four elements named with two meanings.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Zero-level:** the producer sells **directly** to the consumer, as a jaggery maker selling from its **own farm-gate shop**.
2. **One-level:** one middleman, the **retailer**, as a saree weaver selling through **boutiques** in big cities.

questions.stem_md:

questions.solution_md: Meaning; four elements explained and applied.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **promotion mix** is the combination of **advertising, sales promotion, personal selling and publicity** a firm uses to **inform, persuade and remind** buyers.

(b) 1. **Advertising:** a **paid, impersonal** message by an identified sponsor; for example, advertisements in **lifestyle magazines and online** showing its prints.
2. **Sales promotion:** **short-term incentives** to buy now; for example, a **festival discount** or a free cushion cover with every bedspread.
3. **Personal selling:** **face-to-face** presentation; for example, staff explaining the **hand-printing process** to buyers at craft exhibitions.
4. **Publicity:** **unpaid** media coverage; for example, inviting journalists to meet the **women artisans**, which may lead to news features.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between advertising and personal selling on any three bases. [3]
(b) Distinguish between sales promotion and publicity on any two bases. [2]
questions.solution_md: Three bases for (a); two bases for (b).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Nature:** advertising is **impersonal**; personal selling is **face-to-face**.
2. **Flow of communication:** advertising is **one-way**; personal selling is **two-way**, so objections are answered at once.
3. **Reach and cost:** advertising reaches **many people at a low cost per person**; personal selling reaches **few at a high cost per person**.

(b) 1. **Payment and control:** sales promotion is **paid for and controlled** by the firm; publicity is **unpaid** and controlled by the media.
2. **Purpose and duration:** sales promotion gives a **short-term push** to sales through incentives; publicity builds **credibility and awareness** through news over a longer time.
